newsitem.title: ROMANIA: FEATURE - NATO's first round rejects keep hoping.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - NATO's first round rejects keep hoping.

text.p: Languages may be different, but the message from ex-Communist nations likely to be excluded from NATO's first eastward expansion is the same: give us assurance for next time.

Candidates on Europe's northern and southern rims have all but abandoned hopes of quick admission to the Atlantic alliance following a U.S. announcement that it wanted initially to include only the three "favourites" -- Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic.

For some the odds against were very long to start with -- like the Baltic states of Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania, once part of the defunct Soviet empire and whose NATO aspirations particularly raise Moscow's hackles.

In the south, on the Black Sea, Romania has come a long way from an "also ran" less than a year ago to an "almost made it" now. Neighbouring Bulgaria, struggling to put its economy back into shape, is also smarting over the prospect of disappointment at next week's NATO summit in Madrid.

Along the Adriatic coast is tiny and prosperous Slovenia, which stayed out of the bloodbath caused by the split of former Yugoslavia in the early 1990s. The Slovenes, too, did their homework for Madrid.

Even if they do not gain admission in the first wave of newcomers, all these emerging European democracies want a clear signal from Madrid that NATO will also extend its security shield to their region and remove post-World War Two divisions of Europe.
IT'S NOT OVER TILL IT'S OVER
Like the Slovenes, Romanian leaders, buoyed by recent German support, are pressing on for "a reasonable compromise" from NATO's 16-nation summit on July 8-9 in Madrid.
If not outright admission, Madrid should at least produce "a clear date for the second wave, which should be in 1999 or in the year 2000," a senior Romanian official said.

Romanians also argue that a visit by U.S. President Bill Clinton to Bucharest on July 11, the first by an American leader in 20 years, should also put their country on the map as a reliable partner for the United States in the volatile Balkans.

"We are definitely not losers. Even if we don't gain first-wave admission, Romania has shown it is a good fighter and it will fight right up to the end," said Deputy Defence Minister Constantin Dudu Ionescu.
"The battle is over only when the last round has been fired," said Ionescu, a member of the centrist coalition which took office after ending the leftists' seven-year grip on power at the 1996 polls.
"We understood the United States' reasons, but that doesn't mean we should disarm."
WHAT DO WE HAVE TO DO? - BALTICS
On the northern flank, the Baltic states also made a bold lobbying bid, with their Scandinavian friends lending strong support.
But they know their best was not enough, especially with Russia baulking at any notion of an expansion that might include any of the former Soviet republics.
Lithuania, like Estonia and Latvia, wants to be told what it must do to gain membership.
"At this juncture we would like a clear-cut statement (by NATO) of what we have to do," a senior Lithuanian Foreign Ministry official said.
"Our lobby efforts failed because there is still a failure of both parties (NATO and Russia) to recognise what membership for Lithuania would mean, the positive aspects of it," he said.

What the Baltics also hope is that the new Russia-NATO partnership, sealed through a cooperation pact which Moscow signed with the alliance in May in Paris, will augur well for the future of their newly-created democracies.
But,as one diplomat from a NATO country put it, that wish may be pushing things "too far, too fast" -- at least for the Madrid deadline.
SMALL SLOVENIA MAY NOT BE BEAUTIFUL ENOUGH

On the Adriatic front, Italy has led the European chorus supporting Slovenia's membership bid. The former Yugoslav republic has more to offer than its Alpine ski slopes -- a corridor linking Italy to landlocked Hungary.
"However, Slovenia is very small, with a population of two million and an army of about 56,000 men. We have to realise our armed forces have little to offer NATO," a local political analyst said.

"The United States said Slovenia fulfils all conditions for NATO membership and that it would surely be included in the second expansion round," a senior Foreign Ministry official told Reuters in Ljubljana.
To congratulate the new graduates to the NATO security club and sweeten the pill for those who fail the Madrid test, Clinton and his top aides will fan out across the region's capitals after Madrid.

Clinton will go to Poland, Romania and from there to Denmark, a leading supporter of the Baltics' bid. His Secretary of State, Madeleine Albright, goes to Slovenia and also takes in Lithuania to meet the three Baltic leaders after talks with her Russian opposite number in St Petersburg.

U.S. Defence Secretary William Cohen travels to Bulgaria from Hungary and Ukraine -- after Russia the largest former Soviet republic. Ukraine has not applied for membership but will sign a special security charter with NATO at Madrid.
Bulgaria's President Petar Stoyanov, a staunch advocate of his country's admission to NATO, says a "waiting list" of future entrants will be beneficial for Europe's new democracies.

"If we are included in a 'waiting list' this will be an incentive for us to mobilise our efforts fully. Our bid to join NATO is serious and we are not going to give up at the first obstacle," Stoyanov told Reuters in Sofia.
